title: Free and Open Indo-Pacific: A Pillar of Deeper Regional Cooperation
gist: Ten years after Abe's 2016 FOIP proposal, the Quad foreign ministers met with ASEAN in Manila in July 2026 to reaffirm FOIP as a core pillar of cooperation with the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific, underscoring the framework's durability and broad multilateral buy-in across advanced and developing economies.

insights.claim: In July 2026, foreign ministers of the Quad (Japan, the United States, Australia, India) met on the sidelines of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Manila and issued a joint press release reaffirming support for ASEAN centrality, unity, and the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific, while naming FOIP a core pillar of Quad-ASEAN cooperation.
insights.speaker: IIDA Masafumi
insights.so_what: Confirms continued institutional momentum behind the Quad-ASEAN axis in 2026, relevant for gauging the durability of U.S.-aligned regional economic and security architecture versus China-centric alternatives.
insights.quote: issued the “Joint Press Release on Quad Cooperation with ASEAN,” reaffirming their support for ASEAN centrality and unity and the “ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP)”

insights.claim: FOIP marks its tenth anniversary in 2026, having been proposed by then-PM Shinzo Abe at TICAD VI in Nairobi in August 2016 around the principles of freedom from coercion, rule of law, and market economy across an Asia-Africa-Pacific-Indian Ocean region Abe treated as one integrated space.
insights.speaker: IIDA Masafumi
insights.so_what: A decade-long track record signals FOIP is a durable, bipartisan-style Japanese strategic export rather than a transient administration slogan -- useful baseline before assessing 'FOIP 3.0' updates.
insights.quote: Abe viewed Asia and Africa, and the Pacific and Indian Oceans, as an inseparable and integrated region, and expressed Japan’s determination to maintain “freedom from coercion,” the “rule of law,” and a “market economy” across it.

insights.claim: FOIP achieved broad multilateral acceptance across both advanced Western economies (U.S., Australia) and developing nations (African states, India, ASEAN members), and ASEAN itself formally adopted its own Indo-Pacific vision (AOIP) in June 2019 built on ASEAN centrality, inclusiveness, and respect for international law.
insights.speaker: IIDA Masafumi
insights.so_what: Broad-based adoption across developed and developing economies suggests FOIP-aligned infrastructure and trade initiatives have wider addressable buy-in than a narrower US-Japan-only framework would.
insights.quote: The FOIP philosophy won broad acceptance across the Indo-Pacific, from advanced Western nations such as the United States and Australia to developing countries including African nations, India, and ASEAN member states.
